Acceptable levels for wound healing
Serum albumin level of at least 3.0 g/dL
Total lymphocyte count higher than 1,500 cells/mm
Tobacco use impedes wound healing.
Factors associated with the inability of a diabetic foot ulcer to heal
Persistently uncontrolled hyperglycemia
Inability to unload the affected area effectively
Diminished circulation
Infection

Total Protein Level/White Blood Cell Count/Albumin Level
A comprehensive metabolic assessment is paramount to identifying modifiable factors
that influence wound healing. Serum albumin level is a marker of nutritional status.
Albumin is a serum hepatic protein that functions as a transport protein for various
hormones, vitamins, and enzymes. It often is used to gauge whether a patient is
malnourished. Regarding wound healing, patients requiring a transtibial amputation had
lower serum albumin levels than those who underwent successful limb salvage. A serum
albumin level higher than 3.0 g/dL is considered satisfactory for wound healing.1 In
addition, a correlation exists between a total lymphocyte count less than 1.5 × 109 cells/L
and immunocompetence in wound healing.2
Chronic nonhealing wounds often are multifactorial. Smoking results in diminished
circulation and inadequate tissue oxygenation.3 Weight bearing in patients with
diminished sensation results in increased hydrostatic pressure on the foot, leading to a
reduction in blood supply and tissue ischemia.4 Failure to properly offload the affected
area also may lead to infection spread from areas of high pressure to areas lower
pressure along the paths of tendons and their sheaths. Poor glycemic control and
persistent hyperglycemia result in diminished neutrophil and granulocyte function.5
Many diabetic foot ulcers have polymicrobial infection. The most common causative
organisms are gram-positive cocci, such as Staphylococcus aureus.6 In patients with
chronic infections, aerobic gram-negative bacilli often are present. As ulcer depth

Vascular Assessment
Vascular Physical Examination
Pedal pulses
Skin temperature
Coolness may be a sign of peripheral vascular disease.
Warmth may be a sign of venous disease, infection, or neuropathic arthropathy.
Capillary refill
Dependent rubor may be a sign of Charcot neuroarthropathy.
Vascular Assessment Modalities
An ankle-brachial index (ABI) of at least 0.45 and toe pressures higher than 40 mm Hg on
arterial Doppler ultrasonography are considered acceptable levels for healing of diabetic foot
ulcers.
Transcutaneous oxygen measurements higher than 30 mm Hg indicate that blood flow is
adequate for healing.

Vascular Assessment Modalities
Peripheral vascular disease is more common in patients with diabetes mellitus than in
other individuals. A vascular evaluation begins with an examination of the patient’s skin
and palpable dorsalis pedis and tibialis posterior pulses. Thin, shiny, atrophic, and
hairless skin often is indicative of diminished vascularity. Diminished or absent pulses
should prompt a more thorough vascular examination. An acute episode of Charcot
arthropathy can be differentiated from infection because the rubor associated with
Charcot arthropathy often is more pronounced in the dependent position. If the redness
dissipates with elevation of the leg, an infection is less likely.

Vascular assessment modalities include arterial Doppler ultrasonography, the ABI,
transcutaneous oxygen measurements, and angiography. The ABI is commonly used to
diagnose and assess the severity of peripheral vascular disease (Table 1). The ABI is the
systolic pressure of the ankle divided by the systolic pressure of the upper arm. A normal
ABI is between 1.0 and 1.4.8 Calcification of the vessels may falsely elevate the pressures
and result in an ABI higher than 1.4. An ABI lower than 0.9 typically is indicative of
peripheral vascular disease and warrants vascular consultation.

Arterial Doppler ultrasonography is a reproducible method that is effective in assessing
the adequacy of circulation. The results are reported in terms of toe pressure and the
ratio of ankle to arm Doppler arterial pressures. Toe pressures higher than 40 mm Hg
and ankle-brachial ratios higher than 45 mm Hg are considered acceptable levels for
healing.9
Another technique for evaluating healing potential is transcutaneous oxygen tension.
This is a noninvasive test that is performed by assessing the partial pressure of oxygen
beneath the skin and is not falsely elevated by calcified vessels. Transcutaneous oxygen
tension values higher than 30 mm Hg indicate acceptable potential for healing.10 If
screening studies are positive for limb ischemia, angiography can be performed to

Total Contact Cast Indications and Technical Considerations
Total Contact Cast Immobilization and Charcot Restraint Orthotic
Walker
Total contact cast (TCC) immobilization is the preferred method for off-loading plantar
ulcerations and managing acute Charcot arthropathy.
Patients with grade 3 or higher ulcers should undergo incision and drainage and antibiotic
therapy, with wound improvement before TCC immobilization.
TCC immobilization permits an even distribution of foot pressures across the plantar surface
of the foot.
TCC immobilization with guarded ambulation is associated with a mean healing rate of 75%.
Casts should be changed every 2 to 4 weeks until erythema and edema have resolved and the
temperature of the affected limb has decreased and is similar to that of the contralateral limb.
Ulcers should be evaluated, and débridement should be performed at the time of cast
changes.
Radiographs should be obtained every 4 to 6 weeks or more often if an acute change occurs.
TCC immobilization is commonly continued for as long as 4 months.
After the active disease phase has ended, the patient is fitted with a Charcot restraint orthotic
walker and, later, with a custom shoe with orthoses.
A Charcot restraint orthotic walker is a boot composed of a two-piece rigid clamshell with a
rocker bottom and a custom-molded removable insole.
The goal of the insole is to evenly distribute weight and support the ankle joint. Custom
molding allows for even pressure on an abnormally shaped collapsed foot.
Patients who have recovered from Charcot arthropathy subsequently qualify for shoe and
insert provisions of the Therapeutic Shoe Bill to prevent recurrence and ulceration.
Pneumatic Walking Brace
A pneumatic walking brace is an alternative to TCC immobilization. A prefabricated pneumatic
walking brace can be used to reduce forefoot and midfoot plantar pressure.

Pneumatic Walking Brace
TCC immobilization has been the preferred treatment option for pressure off-loading for
diabetic ulcers.11 TCC immobilization is indicated for chronic nonhealing ulcers caused
by neuropathic disorders, including diabetes mellitus, leprosy, and back injury. It also
may be used to reduce foot and lower extremity edema and to allow for consolidation of
Charcot arthropathy. TCC immobilization also is indicated after reconstructive surgery.
Although a relatively simple concept, TCC immobilization requires technical skill to avoid
considerable complications9,12 (Figure 1).

Figure 1
Clinical photographs of a lower extremity show total contact cast application. A, The foot
ulcer is prepared and dressed, with padding placed between the toes to minimize
moisture. B, A stockinette is placed over the lower extremity before additional padding
placement. C, Foam padding is placed over the ulcer and additional pressure points. D,
The ankle is placed in a neutral position and wrapped with the use of cotton undercast
padding from the toes to the tibial tubercle. E, Plaster is applied over the cotton
undercast padding, with reinforcement over the plantar aspect of the foot. F, Fiberglass
cast material is applied in multiple layers over the entire foot in an even distribution.
(Courtesy of Lew Schon, MD, Baltimore, MD.)
The initial cast is placed and maintained for a maximum of 7 days, at which point it must
be removed to assess for any new pressure points and subsequent ulceration. Several
TCC immobilization kits are available on the market. The technique begins with
preparing and dressing the wound and hydrating the skin with the use of an emollient.
The ankle is placed in a neutral position to prevent equinus contracture. Maintenance of
the ankle in a neutral position before application of the padding and cast material is
important to prevent focal pressure points and ulceration. The cast will encapsulate the
entire foot and include the leg up to the tibial tubercle, approximately at the level of the
proximal tibiofibular joint. This will prevent unwanted pressure over the peroneal nerve.
Cotton or lamb’s wool padding is placed between the toes for moisture control. A
stockinette is subsequently rolled over the extremity, with enough excess length to fold
the stockinette over the dorsum of the midfoot distally. The anterior tibial crest and
malleoli are padded. Adhesive foam padding is placed over the forefoot. Cotton
undercast padding is applied to the foot and leg. A thin layer of padding material is
placed to avoid excessive compression after cast material application. Fiberglass cast

material is then placed from distal to proximal in a circumferential fashion. Another layer
of cast material may be placed on the plantar aspect of the cast to add a strength layer,
particularly in heavier patients. Some patients who are permitted to bear weight may
choose to incorporate a rocker bottom sole to facilitate ambulation.
Patients instructed to remain non–weight bearing in the cast for the first 24 hours to
minimize the creation of pressure points on the foot and avoid cast breakage. The TCC is
changed approximately 1 week after initial application, followed by changes every 2
weeks thereafter.
